In practice: initialize with k-means, constrain $\Sigma_k$ diagonal if $d$ is large, beware of singularities (variance $\to 0$). EM will reappear in HMMs (NLP module), VAEs (Deep Learning), probabilistic PCA below, and graph clustering (stochastic block models, Graph ML module).
:::

### 7.3. Principal component analysis

:::: thm
[Theorem 7.6 — PCA: the two viewpoints are equivalent]{.tag} Let $X$ be the centered matrix ($n$ rows, columns of zero mean) and $\hat\Sigma = \tfrac1n X^\top X$. The following two problems have the same solutions — the eigenvectors $v_1, \dots, v_k$ of $\hat\Sigma$ associated with the $k$ largest eigenvalues:

-   **(P1) maximum variance** (solved successively under $v \perp v_1, \dots$):
    $$
    \max \big\{\mathrm{Var}(Xv) : \|v\| = 1\big\} = \max\, v^\top\hat\Sigma v;
    $$
-   **(P2) minimal reconstruction error**, with $P_V$ the orthogonal projection:
    $$
    \min \big\{\sum_i \|x_i - P_V x_i\|^2 : \dim V = k\big\}.
    $$

::: proof
**Rayleigh lemma.** Diagonalize $\hat\Sigma = Q\Lambda Q^\top$ with $\lambda_1 \geq \lambda_2 \geq \dots$. For $\|v\| = 1$,
$$
v^\top\hat\Sigma v = \sum_j \lambda_j c_j^2 \leq \lambda_1 \sum_j c_j^2 = \lambda_1,
$$
reached at $v = v_1$; on the orthogonal of $v_1$, same argument with $\lambda_2$, etc. This is (P1).

**Equivalence.** For $V$ with orthonormal basis $v_1, \dots, v_k$, the projection is a sum of orthogonal projections: $P_V x = \sum_j \langle v_j, x\rangle v_j$ and $\|P_V x\|^2 = \sum_j \langle v_j, x\rangle^2$ (Pythagoras). Hence
$$
\sum_i \|x_i - P_V x_i\|^2 = \sum_i \|x_i\|^2 - \sum_{j=1}^k v_j^\top \hat\Sigma\, v_j\; n = \text{const.} - n\sum_j v_j^\top\hat\Sigma v_j.
$$
Minimizing the reconstruction error ⟺ *maximizing* the sum of the Rayleigh quotients — solved by the same $v_1, \dots, v_k$ (P1).[∎]{.qed}
:::

**SVD.** For $X = U\Sigma V^\top$ (singular value decomposition of the centered matrix), $X^\top X = V\Sigma^2V^\top$: components = columns of $V$, scores $Z = U\Sigma$, variance explained by component $j$ = $\sigma_j^2 \big/ \sum_l \sigma_l^2$.

The choice of $k$ (elbow, cumulative variance) is yet another *capacity* choice — cf. chapter 8.
::::

::: ex
[Probabilistic PCA (PPCA, Tipping & Bishop 1999)]{.tag} Latent variable model: $Z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I_k)$, $X = WZ + \mu + \varepsilon$, $\varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2 I_d)$.

The maximum likelihood is reached at $\hat\mu = \bar x$ and $\hat W$ whose spanned space is *that of the first $k$ principal components* (up to a rotation; the columns are $\sqrt{\lambda_j - \hat\sigma^2}\, v_j$), with $\hat\sigma^2$ = mean of the neglected eigenvalues.

Classical PCA is therefore the limit $\sigma^2 \to 0$ of a generative model; in return, PPCA provides a likelihood (model comparison!), an EM for *missing data*, and mixtures of subspaces. (The complete proof — integrating the marginal law $p(x) = \mathcal{N}(\mu, WW^\top + \sigma^2 I)$ and maximizing — is an excellent exercise; it can be found in the original paper.)
:::

```python
import numpy as np
Xc = X - X.mean(0)
U, S, Vt = np.linalg.svd(Xc, full_matrices=False)
Z = Xc @ Vt[:2].T                  # 2D projection
var_explained = (S**2 / (S**2).sum())[:10]   # variance explained per component
```

::: note
[Spectral PCA → graphs]{.tag} PCA on the adjacency matrix/Laplacian of a graph (*spectral clustering*) is the historical link between classical ML and Graph ML: we will do it again on the Laplacian $L$ in the Graph ML module.
:::

## 8. Generalization theory {#ch8}

This chapter justifies *mathematically* what precedes: when and why does empirical risk minimization generalize? It is the generalization theory of the LLGA track — the [Statistical Learning Theory notes](../m1p1-statistical-learning-theory/index.html), kept for reference, prove in full what is sketched here — and the reading grid for all the hyperparameters of the course (regularization, margin, tree depth, number of boosting iterations).

### 8.1. Why uniform convergence is necessary

:::: prop
[Proposition 8.1 — The estimation gap is controlled by the supremum]{.tag} Let
$$
f_\mathcal{F} \in \arg\min_{f \in \mathcal{F}} \mathcal{R}(f).
$$
Then
$$
\mathcal{R}(\hat f_n) - \mathcal{R}(f_\mathcal{F}) \ \leq\ 2\, \sup_{f \in \mathcal{F}}\ \big|\, \hat{\mathcal{R}}_n(f) - \mathcal{R}(f) \,\big|.
$$

::: proof
Interleave the empirical risk:
$$
\mathcal{R}(\hat f_n) - \mathcal{R}(f_\mathcal{F}) = \big[\mathcal{R}(\hat f_n) - \hat{\mathcal{R}}_n(\hat f_n)\big] + \big[\hat{\mathcal{R}}_n(\hat f_n) - \hat{\mathcal{R}}_n(f_\mathcal{F})\big] + \big[\hat{\mathcal{R}}_n(f_\mathcal{F}) - \mathcal{R}(f_\mathcal{F})\big].
$$
The middle term is $\leq 0$ (definition of ERM); the other two are bounded by the supremum.[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Example 8.2 — When pointwise convergence is not enough: the sinusoids]{.tag} Take $\mathcal{X} = [0, 2\pi]$, $Y \in \{-1, +1\}$ balanced, and the class
$$
\mathcal{F} = \{x \mapsto \mathrm{sign}(\sin(\omega x)) : \omega > 0\}.
$$
For *every* sample $x_1 < \cdots < x_n$ and *every* label $y \in \{-1,+1\}^n$, there exists $\omega$ such that $\mathrm{sign}(\sin(\omega x_i)) = y_i$ for every $i$ (choose $\omega$ large enough to fit an alternation between each pair of consecutive points).

ERM therefore reaches $\hat{\mathcal{R}}_n = 0$ *always*, whereas for a fixed $f$, $\mathcal{R}(f) = 1/2$ (perfect decorrelation of the signs): Hoeffding (theorem 0.3) holds *for each fixed $f$*, but the supremum over $\mathcal{F}$ equals $1/2$. Without *uniform* control, learning proves nothing.
:::

### 8.2. Vapnik-Chervonenkis dimension

::: def
[Definition 8.3 — Shattering and VC dimension]{.tag} A class $\mathcal{F}$ of classifiers *shatters* the points $x_1, \dots, x_n$ if every label of $\{-1,+1\}^n$ is realizable by some $f \in \mathcal{F}$. The **growth function** is
$$
\Pi_\mathcal{F}(n) = \max_{x_1, \dots, x_n} \#\{(\mathrm{sign}\,f(x_1), \dots, \mathrm{sign}\,f(x_n)) : f \in \mathcal{F}\}.
$$
The **VC dimension** is
$$
d_{\mathrm{VC}} = \max\{n : \Pi_\mathcal{F}(n) = 2^n\}
$$
(possibly $+\infty$).
:::

::: ex
[Examples 8.4 — Three VC dimensions computed by hand]{.tag}

-   **(i) Thresholds on $\mathbb{R}$**, $f_t = \mathbf{1}\{x \leq t\}$:
    $$
    d_{\mathrm{VC}} = 1.
    $$
    One point is shattered ($t$ before/after). Two points $x_1 < x_2$ are not: the label $(0, 1)$ would require $x_1 > t$ and $x_2 \leq t$, impossible.
-   **(ii) Intervals** $f_{a,b} = \mathbf{1}\{x \in [a, b]\}$:
    $$
    d_{\mathrm{VC}} = 2.
    $$
    Two points: all labels (via an empty $[a,b]$, enclosing, or exactly fitted); three points $x_1 < x_2 < x_3$: the label $(1, 0, 1)$ is unrealizable (an interval containing $x_1, x_3$ contains $x_2$).
-   **(iii) Affine hyperplanes in $\mathbb{R}^d$**:
    $$
    d_{\mathrm{VC}} = d + 1.
    $$
    The $d+1$ vertices of a simplex are shattered (to each vertex associate the hyperplane through the opposite face); $d + 2$ points never are — this is Radon's theorem: any family of $d+2$ points can be partitioned into two subsets with intersecting convex hulls, and no hyperplane can separate this partition.
-   **(iv)** Example 8.2 shows a class of infinite VC dimension — which learns nothing.
:::

::: thm
[Lemma 8.5 — Sauer-Shelah lemma (statement)]{.tag} If $d_{\mathrm{VC}}(\mathcal{F}) = d$, then for every $n \geq d$,
$$
\Pi_\mathcal{F}(n) \ \leq\ \sum_{i=0}^{d} \binom{n}{i} \ \leq\ \Big(\frac{e\,n}{d}\Big)^{d}.
$$
*Intuition*: a class of dimension $d$ can realize only labels "determined" by at most $d$ points — the growth is polynomial of degree $d$ in $n$, not exponential. (Proof by induction on $n + d$, exercise; cf. Shalev-Shwartz & Ben-David, ch. 7.)
:::

### 8.3. The VC bound by double sampling (sketch)

:::: thm
[Theorem 8.6 — Vapnik-Chervonenkis bound]{.tag} With probability at least $1 - \delta$ over the sample, *simultaneously for every* $f \in \mathcal{F}$ (loss in $[0,1]$, VC dimension $d$, $n \geq d$):
$$
\mathcal{R}(f) \ \leq\ \hat{\mathcal{R}}_n(f) + \sqrt{\frac{8\,\big(d \log \tfrac{2 e n}{d} + \log \tfrac{4}{\delta}\big)}{n}}.
$$

::: proof
*Sketch in three moves — the Vapnik-Chervonenkis double-sampling argument.*

1.  **Ghost sample.** Draw $2n$ iid points and split into two halves $S, S'$ with empirical risks $\hat R_S, \hat R_{S'}$. By Hoeffding (theorem 0.3), each is within $\varepsilon/4$ of $\mathcal{R}$ with high probability.

    Consequently, if some $f$ commits
    $$
    \hat{\mathcal{R}}_S(f) + \varepsilon \leq \mathcal{R}(f),
    $$
    then $\hat R_S(f)$ and $\hat R_{S'}(f)$ differ by at least $\varepsilon/2$: we have replaced the unobservable risk $\mathcal{R}$ by a *second observable sample*.

2.  **Symmetrization by permutations.** Conditionally on the $2n$ points, the labels $f(x_i)$ of a given $f$ take only $\Pi_\mathcal{F}(2n)$ values.

    By randomly swapping the roles $S \leftrightarrow S'$ (random permutation), the probability that a *better* $f$ of the class separates the two halves by $\varepsilon/2$ is bounded by
    $$
    2\,\Pi_\mathcal{F}(2n)\, e^{-n\varepsilon^2/8}:
    $$
    a simple counting over the $\Pi_\mathcal{F}(2n)$ distinct behaviors, each subject to a binomial Hoeffding.

3.  **Sauer.** Bound $\Pi_\mathcal{F}(2n) \leq (2en/d)^d$, solve in $\varepsilon$ the inequality
    $$
    (2en/d)^d e^{-n\varepsilon^2/8} \leq \delta:
    $$
    this is the announced square root.[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: note
[Reading the bound]{.tag} The excess risk is $\mathcal{O}\big(\sqrt{d/n}\,\big)$ up to logarithmic constants: to divide the error by two, one needs four times more data — or a class four times smaller. Practical rules: (i) $n \gg d$ is the healthy regime; (ii) *capacity control* (reduce the effective $d$ by regularization, margin, sparsity) pays as much as more data; (iii) the bound is conservative — it explains, it does not predict exact performance.
:::

### 8.4. Rademacher complexity

::: def
[Definition 8.7 — Empirical Rademacher complexity]{.tag} For a sample $S = (x_1, \dots, x_n)$ and iid Rademacher variables $\sigma_i$ uniform on $\{-1, +1\}$: $$\hat{\mathcal{R}}_S(\mathcal{F}) = \mathbb{E}_\sigma\Big[\sup_{f \in \mathcal{F}} \frac1n \sum_{i=1}^n \sigma_i f(x_i)\Big].$$ This is the capacity of $\mathcal{F}$ to "fit the noise": if a class can align itself with purely random labels, it will also memorize your data.
:::

::: thm
[Theorem 8.8 — Oracle bounds via Rademacher]{.tag} For an $L$-Lipschitz loss, with probability $\geq 1 - \delta$:
$$
\mathcal{R}(\hat f_n) \ \leq\ \inf_{f \in \mathcal{F}} \mathcal{R}(f) + 2\, L\, \mathbb{E}_S\big[\hat{\mathcal{R}}_S(\mathcal{F})\big] + \sqrt{\tfrac{\log(1/\delta)}{2n}},
$$
and for bounded linear classes
$$
\mathcal{F}_R = \{x \mapsto \langle\theta, x\rangle : \|\theta\| \leq R, \|x\| \leq 1\}:
$$
$\hat{\mathcal{R}}_S(\mathcal{F}_R) \leq R/\sqrt n$ (computation of theorem 3.6).

*Sketch.*

-   **(i)** symmetrization by a ghost sample (as in 8.3, without counting this time — the supremum stays on the empirical side);
-   **(ii)** Ledoux-Talagrand contraction lemma: composing with a Lipschitz loss only multiplies the complexity by the constant $L$.[∎]{.qed}
:::

Rademacher versus VC: the Rademacher complexity is *data-dependent* (it is computed on the sample, by simulating the $\sigma_i$), without a logarithmic factor, and applies to continuous classes of real-valued functions (scores, margins). It is the standard tool of modern bounds — including the SVM margin bounds (theorem 3.6) and the aggregation bounds of chapter 9.

### 8.5. Regularizing = controlling capacity

::: note
[Why this is central in ML]{.tag} Reread the course:

-   ridge and lasso constrain $\|\theta\|$ — and the norm-$R$ ball has Rademacher complexity $R/\sqrt n$ (theorem 8.8);
-   the SVM maximizes the margin $\gamma$, which divides the complexity by $\gamma$ (theorem 3.6);
-   boosting stops early, limiting the effective size of the tree dictionary;
-   tree pruning (6.1) and rank selection in PCA (7.3) do the same.

This is **structural risk minimization**: a scale of nested classes $\mathcal{F}_1 \subset \mathcal{F}_2 \subset \cdots$, each with its complexity $\mathcal{R}_n(\mathcal{F}_j)$, and a trade-off tuned on data $\hat{\mathcal{R}}_n(f) + \text{complexity}$. The "lambda" you tune in the labs is exactly this theory-practice slider.
:::

## 9. Research at CMAP and LIX (Le Pennec, Read) {#ch9}

At École Polytechnique, two research lines extend this module directly: multi-label classification (Jesse Read, LIX) and estimator aggregation (Erwan Le Pennec, CMAP). Two topics where the previous chapters reappear — and gateways to internships / PhD topics.

### 9.1. Jesse Read: learning sets of labels (multi-label, streams, extreme)

::: def
[Definition 9.1 — Multi-label problem]{.tag} Each example $x$ is associated with a *set* of labels $Y \subseteq \{1, \dots, L\}$, viewed as a vector of $\{0,1\}^L$. One learns $h : \mathcal{X} \to \{0,1\}^L$. Usual losses: **Hamming** (error rate per label, $\frac1L\sum_j \mathbf{1}\{h_j(x) \neq y_j\}$) and **subset accuracy** (*subset accuracy*: the whole vector must be correct). Applications: text tagging, genomics, recommendation — cf. exercise 10, project [P3](#proj-3) and the NLP module.
:::

The **taxonomy** popularized by Jesse Read's thesis (*Scalable Multi-label Classification*, Waikato, 2010) and by the classifier chains paper separates methods into two families: *problem transformation* (bring multi-label back to standard binary/multiclass problems) and *algorithm adaptation* (modify kNN, trees, SVMs... to directly ingest label vectors). Three canonical transformations:

| Method | Principle | Strength / weakness |
|---|---|---|
| Binary Relevance (BR) | $L$ independent binary classifiers $h_j(x)$ | simple, parallelizable; ignores dependencies between labels |
| Label Powerset (LP) | each observed combination = one class of a single multiclass problem | captures all dependencies; explosion of rare classes ($\leq 2^L$) |
| Classifier Chains (CC) | $h_j$ predicts $y_j$ from $(x, y_1, \dots, y_{j-1})$ | captures conditional dependencies; sensitive to order and to cascading errors |

::: ex
[Example 9.2 — Classifier chains on a mini-corpus]{.tag} Three labels: $S$ (science), $P$ (politics), $s$ (health). Corpus:

  Document                      $S$   $P$   $s$
  ----------------------------- ----- ----- -----
  article 1 (climate)           1     0     1
  article 2 (election)          0     1     0
  article 3 (research budget)   1     1     0
  article 4 (sports)            0     0     0

The pattern "$S = 1, P = 0 \Rightarrow s = 1$" (non-politicized science articles: health) is invisible to BR, each of whose binary classifiers sees only $x$. For a chain of order $(S, P, s)$, the last link learns $h_s(x, S, P)$ — the dependency becomes a simple additional *feature*, and the classifier of chapter 3 applies as is.

At prediction time, one propagates: $\hat S = h_S(x)$, then $\hat P = h_P(x, \hat S)$, then $\hat s = h_s(x, \hat S, \hat P)$.

Two remedies to the arbitrary order and to cascading error: **ensembles of chains** (random orders, average vote — the bagging of chapter 6, again) and the probabilistic route (predict the expectation over the $2^L$ paths or sample).
:::

::: note
[From multi-label to massive data: streaming and extreme]{.tag} Three extensions carried by Jesse Read and his co-authors, which join chapter 4:

-   **(i) Multi-label streams** (Read, Bifet, Pfahringer, Holmes, *Scalable and Efficient Multi-label Classification for Evolving Data Streams*, Machine Learning, 2012): data arrive continuously, a single pass, bounded memory — one learns incremental multi-output regression trees (iSOUP-Tree) and one predicts score vectors label by label. Concept drift is treated there as a temporal structure: *Concept-drifting data streams are time series* (arXiv:1810.02266).
-   **(ii) Extreme classification**: $L$ on the order of $10^5$ to $10^6$ (labels = Wikipedia articles, listings; see the research notes of [RL ch. 8](../m1p2-reinforcement-learning/index.html#ch8)); BR (one-vs-rest) becomes relevant again because label embeddings factorize the sparse matrix — reviewed in *Deep Learning for Multi-label Classification* (arXiv:1502.05988).
-   **(iii) Tools**: the *River* library — machine learning for streams in Python (Montiel, Halford, Salles, ..., Read et al., JMLR 22(110), 2021) implements these methods; the meta-challenge there is the evaluation protocol (prequential, sliding window), defined in [RL ch. 8](../m1p2-reinforcement-learning/index.html#ch8), definition 8.3.
:::

### 9.2. Erwan Le Pennec: aggregating estimators rather than choosing one

Facing a family $f_1, \dots, f_M$ of candidate estimators (different kernels, different wavelet bases, different values of $\lambda$...), the classical statistician *selects* one. The alternative carried by Erwan Le Pennec and his co-authors is to *aggregate* them: predict with a weighted combination $f_{\hat\pi} = \sum_m \hat\pi_m f_m$, the weights being learned from data — typically **exponential weights** (Gibbs measure):

::: key
[Key result — exponential weights]{.tag}
$$
\hat\pi_m \ \propto\ \exp\big(-\lambda\, n\, \hat{\mathcal{R}}_n(f_m)\big), \qquad \sum_m \hat\pi_m = 1.
$$
:::

The risk of the aggregate is then controlled by an *oracle inequality*: pay the price of the *best* candidate up to a $\log M$ term, with no assumption on which one is best.

::: ex
[Example 9.3 — Two estimators, exponential weights]{.tag} $M = 2$, empirical risks $\hat{\mathcal{R}}_n(f_1) = 0.30$ and $\hat{\mathcal{R}}_n(f_2) = 0.38$, $n = 100$, $\lambda = 1$:
$$
\hat\pi_1/\hat\pi_2 = \exp\big(n\lambda(0.38 - 0.30)\big) = e^{8} \approx 3000;
$$
the aggregate ≈ $f_1$. With $n = 10$: ratio $e^{0.8} \approx 2.2$, an almost uniform mixture.

Moral: $\lambda$ tunes the *selectivity* according to the amount of data — exactly the role of the temperature in Gibbs mechanisms, and we recover the softmax formula of chapter 3. If a third candidate emerges on fresh data, the aggregate will rebalance — a robustness that a hard selection (argmin) does not have.
:::

::: prop
[Typical result (Montuelle & Le Pennec, 2014/2019)]{.tag} In the fixed-design regression model, for a *generic* collection of *linear* estimators (projections, ridge, thresholding algorithms, wavelet thresholding estimators...), the PAC-Bayesian aggregation procedure with exponential weights satisfies an oracle inequality *in probability*: with probability $1 - \delta$, the risk of the aggregate is less than the risk of the best estimator of the collection plus an explicit remainder in $\sqrt{\log(M/\delta)/n}$.

The guarantee holds no longer only in expectation: the in-probability guarantee, a finer one, is the specific contribution of this work (long version: *PAC-Bayesian aggregation of linear estimators*, Nonparametric Statistics, 2019; preprint arXiv:1410.0661). Aggregation is *robust to the worst case*: one never bets on a single candidate.
:::

::: note
[Connection with the rest of the course]{.tag} The guiding thread is the same:

-   **bagging** (theorem 6.2) = aggregation with uniform weights of bootstrap versions of one estimator;
-   **boosting** (6.3) = *iterative* construction of the dictionary, each tree receiving a weight;
-   **exponential weights** = the update mechanism of AdaBoost and Gibbs algorithms;
-   **regularization** (8.5) = why the aggregate generalizes better than the best *empirical* candidate.

On this last point, Erwan Le Pennec's nonparametric statistics provides the guardrails: optimal kernel selection for density estimation, *needlet* thresholding for models with random coefficients (with É. Gautier), estimation of copula densities by thresholding (with F. Autin and K. Tribouley, 2010) — always the same grammar: a *dictionary*, a *penalty*, an *oracle inequality*. NL-Means image denoising can be reread this way as a local aggregation of kernel estimators (Salmon & Le Pennec, 2009).
:::

## Exercises {#ex}

1.  **★ Closed-form ridge.** Show that $\hat\theta_{\text{ridge}}$ is indeed given by $(X^\top X + n\lambda I)^{-1}X^\top y$ by setting the gradient to zero, then that the problem is always strictly convex as soon as $\lambda > 0$.

    ::: proof
    [Solution]{.tag} Gradient:
    $$
    \nabla_\theta\big(\tfrac1n\|y - X\theta\|^2 + \lambda\|\theta\|_2^2\big) = \tfrac2n X^\top(X\theta - y) + 2\lambda\theta;
    $$
    setting it to zero gives $(X^\top X + n\lambda I)\theta = X^\top y$.

    The Hessian $\tfrac2n(X^\top X + n\lambda I) \succeq 2\lambda I \succ 0$ is positive definite for $\lambda > 0$, even if $X^\top X$ is singular: unique global minimum — this is the first practical benefit of regularization (cf. proposition 2.5 for the spectral reading).[∎]{.qed}
    :::
2.  **★ Gauss-Markov in dimension 1.** Model $y_i = \theta + \varepsilon_i$, $\varepsilon_i$ centered, independent, with variance $\sigma^2$. Show that among the linear unbiased estimators $a^\top y$ of $\theta$, the empirical mean has minimal variance.

    ::: proof
    [Solution]{.tag} Unbiasedness:
    $$
    \mathbb{E}[a^\top y] = \theta\,\textstyle\sum_i a_i = \theta
    $$
    for every $\theta$, hence $\sum_i a_i = 1$. Variance: $\mathrm{Var}(a^\top y) = \sigma^2\|a\|^2$.

    Minimize $\|a\|^2$ under the constraint $\mathbf{1}^\top a = 1$ with a Lagrange multiplier $\nu$ ([section 0.3](#constrained-opt)). Stationarity of the Lagrangian
    $$
    \|a\|^2 - \nu(\mathbf 1^\top a - 1)
    $$
    gives $2a_i = \nu$ for every $i$: all the $a_i$ are equal, and the constraint gives the uniform $a_i = 1/n$. This is the case $X = \mathbf 1$ of theorem 2.3; the estimator $\frac1n\sum y_i$ is its geometric projection.[∎]{.qed}
    :::
3.  **★ Cross-entropy.** Verify that minimizing the logistic cross-entropy amounts to maximizing the Bernoulli likelihood
    $$
    \prod_i \sigma(\theta^\top x_i)^{y_i}(1-\sigma)^{1-y_i},
    $$
    and compute
    $$
    \nabla_\theta \hat{\mathcal{R}}_n = \frac1n X^\top(\sigma(X\theta) - y).
    $$
    (All the steps are in theorem 3.3: redo them without notes.)
4.  **★ Bagging and correlation.** Derive again the formula
    $$
    \mathrm{Var}(A_B) = \rho\sigma^2 + \tfrac{1-\rho}{B}\sigma^2
    $$
    of theorem 6.2, then comment: what happens if the $B$ trees are identical ($\rho = 1$)? Why does a small $m_{\text{try}}$ decrease $\rho$ — and at what price?

    ::: proof
    [Solution]{.tag} Expand the variance of the sum with equicorrelated covariances $\tfrac1{B^2}[B\sigma^2 + B(B-1)\rho\sigma^2]$. If $\rho = 1$, all the trees are identical: the variance remains $\sigma^2$, bagging is useless. Reducing $m_{\text{try}}$ randomizes the candidate splits and decorrelates the trees; in exchange, each tree, seeing fewer variables, may miss the "right" split — its individual bias increases slightly. The optimal trade-off is found by validation (chapter 4).[∎]{.qed}
    :::
5.  **★★ Kernel duel.** (i) Show that $k(x, x') = (\langle x, x'\rangle + 1)^2$ on $\mathcal{X} = \mathbb{R}^2$ is a kernel by exhibiting an explicit feature map. (ii) Is the function $k(x,x') = \cos(x - x')$ on $\mathbb{R}$ a positive definite kernel?

    ::: proof
    [Solution]{.tag} **(i)** Expand:
    $$
    (x_1x'_1 + x_2x'_2 + 1)^2 = x_1^2x_1'^2 + 2x_1x_1'x_2x_2' + x_2^2x_2'^2 + 2x_1x'_1 + 2x_2x'_2 + 1 = \langle \phi(x), \phi(x')\rangle
    $$
    with
    $$
    \phi(x) = (x_1^2,\ \sqrt2\,x_1x_2,\ x_2^2,\ \sqrt2\,x_1,\ \sqrt2\,x_2,\ 1)
    $$
    — dimension 6 versus 2: the kernel trick saves the explicit passage.

    **(ii)** Yes, by the addition formula:
    $$
    \cos(x - x') = \cos x\cos x' + \sin x \sin x' = \langle(\cos x, \sin x),\,(\cos x', \sin x')\rangle.
    $$
    A dimension-2 feature map, unit norm.[∎]{.qed}
    :::
6.  **★★ Dual derivation of the SVM.** Take up the primal of theorem 3.5: write the Lagrangian with multipliers $(\alpha_i, \mu_i)$, set the gradients in $(\theta, b, \xi)$ to zero, and recover (a) the dual function, (b) the three families of points of the table in section 3.2 via the complementarity conditions.
7.  **★★ EM for a mixture of two 1D Gaussians.** Write the two steps, implement (NumPy), and check on a mixture $0.4\,\mathcal{N}(-2, 1) + 0.6\,\mathcal{N}(3, 1)$ that the log-likelihood is increasing over 50 iterations (theorem 7.5: plot $\log p_{\theta_t}$ and check the increase, strict away from a stationary point).
8.  **★★ VC by hand.** (i) Show that the intervals $[a,b]$ of $\mathbb{R}$ do not shatter 3 aligned points (example 8.4(ii)). (ii) Compute the VC bound (theorem 8.6) for $d = 10$, $n = 1000$, $\delta = 5\%$ and comment ("how much data per dimension?").

    ::: proof
    [Solution]{.tag} **(i)** For $x_1 < x_2 < x_3$, the label $(1,0,1)$ is unrealizable: an interval containing $x_1$ and $x_3$ contains the whole interval $[x_1, x_3]$, hence $x_2$.

    **(ii)** The bound is
    $$
    \sqrt{8(10\log(2e \cdot 1000/10) + \log 80)/1000} \approx \sqrt{8 \times (63.0 + 4.4)/1000} \approx 0.73:
    $$
    a theoretical error margin of 73 points! The bound is (very) conservative — it guarantees the *consistency* of the ERM principle (error $\to 0$ as $n/d \to \infty$), not actual performance; this is why one also evaluates by cross-validation (4.2).[∎]{.qed}
    :::
9.  **★★ k-means++.** Explain why the naive initialization can cost $\mathcal{O}(\log k)$ times the optimum (give an example: clusters of very unequal sizes), and simulate both initializations on anisotropic blobs while measuring the ratio $W_{\text{final}}/W^\star$ (proposition 7.3: aim for the guarantee $8(\ln k + 2)$).
10. **★★ Multi-label: Hamming versus subset accuracy.** On example 9.2 (labels $S, P, s$), one tests on 10 documents of which 6 follow the pattern "$S=1, P=0 \Rightarrow s=1$" and 4 are "all zero". BR learns $h_s \equiv 0$ (it sees only $x$), CC learns $h_s(x, S=1, P=0) = 1$. Compute the Hamming and subset accuracy losses of the two methods, and explain when BR becomes competitive again.

    ::: proof
    [Solution]{.tag} CC is perfect on the learned patterns: Hamming $0$, accuracy $1$.

    BR errs on the label $s$ of the 6 "pure science" documents: Hamming $= \frac{6}{10 \times 3} = 0.2$, accuracy $= \frac4{10} = 0.4$.

    If the $S \to s$ dependency did not exist (labels conditionally independent given $x$), BR would be optimal for Hamming — the chain would only add noise; it is the targeted loss (Hamming *vs* fine dependencies) that dictates the method (table in section 9.1).[∎]{.qed}
    :::
11. **★★ Fairness audit on census data.** The [`folktables`](https://github.com/socialfoundations/folktables) package (MIT licence; data: US Census Bureau [ACS public-use microdata](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/microdata.html)) builds the ACSIncome task: predict whether a person's income exceeds USD 50,000. Load one state and year (for example California, 2018), and keep sex and race as sensitive attributes.

    (i) Fit a logistic regression and a gradient-boosting model inside a pipeline (section 4.3) and report their accuracy. (ii) For each sex and each race group, report the positive rate, TPR, FPR and PPV with 95% bootstrap intervals (section 4.8). (iii) Check the identity of proposition 4.5 on your numbers. (iv) On a validation split, choose one threshold per sex that equalizes the TPRs, and report the accuracy lost on the test split. (v) Which gaps exceed their intervals, and what would deploying group-wise thresholds require?
12. **★★★ Exponential weights.** Three estimators with empirical risks $0.30$, $0.32$, $0.50$, $n = 100$.

    Compute the weights $\hat\pi$ for $\lambda \in \{0.1\,;\ 1\,;\ 10\}$ (definition in chapter 9) and plot $\max_m \hat\pi_m$ as a function of $\lambda$. What link with the softmax of chapter 3, and what role does $\lambda$ play when one doubts the validity of the empirical risks (small $n$)?

    ::: proof
    [Solution]{.tag} Weights $\propto \exp(-100\lambda \hat R_m)$:

    -   for $\lambda = 0.1$, ratios $e^{-0.2} \approx 0.82$ and $e^{-2} \approx 0.14$ (soft mixture);
    -   for $\lambda = 1$, $e^{-2} \approx 0.14$ and $e^{-20} \approx 2\cdot10^{-9}$;
    -   for $\lambda = 10$, quasi-hard selection.

    This is a softmax on the scores $-n\lambda\hat R_m$ — $\lambda$ plays the role of the inverse temperature. At small $n$, the $\hat R_m$ are noisy (chapter 0): taking $\lambda$ small keeps a mixture, robust to estimation error — precisely the logic of the oracle inequalities of chapter 9.[∎]{.qed}
    :::
13. **★★★ Running project.** On the *20 Newsgroups* dataset (count vectorizer → TF-IDF → logistic/forest), build the complete pipeline with *nested* cross-validation (4.2), report the confusion matrix and macro F1, and calibrate the probabilities (4.5) before choosing the decision threshold.

    TF-IDF multiplies each word count by the logarithm of the inverse fraction of documents that contain the word ([NLP ch. 2](../m1p2-nlp-text-mining/index.html#ch2)). The NLP module of Period 2 takes the same task up with linear models ([ch. 3](../m1p2-nlp-text-mining/index.html#ch3)) and transformers ([ch. 7](../m1p2-nlp-text-mining/index.html#ch7)); [project P3](#proj-3) extends it to multi-label tagging.

The projects below are optional practice, ungraded unless the teaching team decides otherwise.

### A classical assessment {#projects-exam}

The official mode is one final exam, so this proposal puts the whole grade on a written paper. Labs, exercises and projects stay formative: they prepare the paper, which tests the in-class chapters.

| Component | Weight | Format | Covers |
|---|---|---|---|
| Written final exam | 100 % | 3 h, no computer, no documents; the formulas of theorems 8.6 and 8.8 are printed on the paper | ch. 0–8 (ch. 9, self-study, is not examined) |
| Labs, exercises, projects | 0 % (formative) | written feedback on request | sessions 1–12, Ex. 1–13, projects P1–P4 |

**Resit.** The LLGA section of the sheet shows no resit rule; for the other degrees of the sheet a resit is allowed. A resit consistent with the session plan is a written exam of the same format on ch. 0–8.

**Sample questions.** The six questions below form one complete 3-hour paper of 20 points; each tests an in-class chapter, and they mix derivations, a hand computation and two diagnoses.

**Q1 (3 pts) — Risk decomposition.** Let $\hat f_n$ be the empirical risk minimizer in a class $\mathcal{F}$ and $\mathcal{R}^\star$ the Bayes risk. (a) Write the excess risk as an approximation error plus an estimation error. (b) How does each term move when $\mathcal{F}$ grows, and when $n$ grows? (c) A model has 2% training error and 25% test error: which term dominates, and what are two remedies?

::: proof
[Marking points]{.tag}

-   The decomposition of chapter 1, with both terms named (1 pt):
    $$
    \mathcal{R}(\hat f_n) - \mathcal{R}^\star = \Big[\inf_{f \in \mathcal{F}} \mathcal{R}(f) - \mathcal{R}^\star\Big] + \Big[\mathcal{R}(\hat f_n) - \inf_{f \in \mathcal{F}} \mathcal{R}(f)\Big].
    $$
-   A larger $\mathcal{F}$ lowers (or keeps) the approximation term and raises the estimation term; a larger $n$ lowers the estimation term only (1 pt).
-   The large train–test gap is overfitting: the estimation term dominates. Two remedies among regularization (chapter 2), a smaller class, early stopping, more data (1 pt). Common error: claiming that more data reduces the approximation error.
:::

**Q2 (4 pts) — Ridge in closed form.** For $\lambda > 0$, minimize
$$
J(\theta) = \tfrac1n\|y - X\theta\|^2 + \lambda\|\theta\|^2 .
$$
Compute the gradient, give the minimizer, and show that it is unique even when $p > n$. Then give the factor by which ridge shrinks each singular direction of $X$.

::: proof
[Marking points]{.tag}

-   Gradient (1 pt):
    $$
    \nabla J(\theta) = \tfrac2n X^\top(X\theta - y) + 2\lambda\theta .
    $$
-   Setting it to zero gives $\hat\theta = (X^\top X + n\lambda I)^{-1}X^\top y$ (1 pt).
-   The Hessian $\tfrac2n(X^\top X + n\lambda I) \succeq 2\lambda I \succ 0$: $J$ is strictly convex and the minimizer is unique, whatever the rank of $X$ (1 pt).
-   With the SVD $X = U\,\mathrm{diag}(\sigma_j)\,V^\top$, direction $v_j$ is shrunk by $\sigma_j^2/(\sigma_j^2 + n\lambda)$ relative to least squares (proposition 2.5) (1 pt). Common error: dropping the factor $n$ that comes from the $1/n$ normalization.
:::

**Q3 (3 pts) — Logistic regression is convex.** With labels $y'_i \in \{-1, +1\}$, let
$$
L(\theta) = \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n \log\big(1 + e^{-y'_i\theta^\top x_i}\big).
$$
Compute the gradient and the Hessian, conclude that $L$ is convex, and give a condition for strict convexity.

::: proof
[Marking points]{.tag}

-   Gradient (1 pt):
    $$
    \nabla L(\theta) = -\frac1n\sum_i y'_i\,\sigma(-y'_i\theta^\top x_i)\,x_i .
    $$
-   Hessian, using $y_i'^2 = 1$ and $\sigma(z)\sigma(-z) = \sigma(z)(1 - \sigma(z))$ (1 pt):
    $$
    \nabla^2 L(\theta) = \frac1n\sum_i \sigma(\theta^\top x_i)\big(1 - \sigma(\theta^\top x_i)\big)\,x_i x_i^\top .
    $$
-   Each term is positive semidefinite, so $L$ is convex; the weights are positive, so $L$ is strictly convex as soon as the $x_i$ span $\mathbb{R}^d$, i.e. $\ker X = \{0\}$ (theorem 3.3) (1 pt). Common error: claiming strict convexity without the rank condition.
:::

**Q4 (3 pts) — Lloyd's algorithm.** Show that the k-means cost $W$ never increases along Lloyd's iterations and that the algorithm stops after finitely many iterations. Does it reach the global minimum?

::: proof
[Marking points]{.tag}

-   Assignment step: with the centers fixed, sending each point to its nearest center minimizes each term of $W$ (1 pt).
-   Update step: with the partition fixed, the barycenter minimizes $\sum_{i \in S}\|x_i - \mu\|^2$, by Huygens' identity (theorem 7.2) (1 pt).
-   $W$ is non-increasing and strictly decreases whenever a point moves to a strictly closer center or a center moves; there are at most $k^n$ partitions, so the algorithm stops — at a stationary point, not necessarily the global minimum, hence k-means++ and restarts (1 pt). Common error: arguing from a convexity of $W$, which is not jointly convex.
:::

**Q5 (4 pts) — VC dimension of intervals, and what the bound says.** (a) Show that the indicators of intervals $[a, b] \subset \mathbb{R}$ have VC dimension 2. (b) Evaluate the deviation term of theorem 8.6 (formula printed on the paper) for $d = 2$, $n = 10{,}000$ and $\delta = 0.05$. (c) Interpret the number.

::: proof
[Marking points]{.tag}

-   Two points $x_1 < x_2$ are shattered: the four labelings are obtained with an empty interval, $\{x_1\}$, $\{x_2\}$ and $[x_1, x_2]$ (1 pt).
-   Three points $x_1 < x_2 < x_3$ cannot receive $(1, 0, 1)$: an interval containing $x_1$ and $x_3$ contains $x_2$ (1 pt).
-   With natural logarithms, $2\log(2e \cdot 10^4/2) = 20.42$ and $\log(4/0.05) = 4.38$ (1 pt), so
    $$
    \sqrt{8 \times (20.42 + 4.38)/10^4} \approx 0.14 .
    $$
-   With probability at least 0.95, the risk of *every* interval classifier exceeds its empirical risk by at most 0.14; the bound is conservative but not vacuous here, and it shrinks like $\sqrt{d/n}$ (1 pt). Common error: base-10 logarithms, which give 0.09.
:::

**Q6 (3 pts) — Diagnosing an evaluation.** A colleague has 50 samples and 5,000 features with labels that are in fact random. She standardizes the data, keeps the 20 features most correlated with the label, then reports a 5-fold cross-validated accuracy of 0.90 for logistic regression. Explain the result, give the correct protocol, and say what accuracy it should report.

::: proof
[Marking points]{.tag}

-   The selection (and the scaling) was fitted on all 50 samples, so it saw the test folds; among 5,000 noise features, the largest sample correlations are about 0.6, so the selected features look predictive (example 4.3) (1 pt).
-   Correct protocol: put the scaler and `SelectKBest` in a `Pipeline` refitted on the training part of each fold, nested if $k$ is tuned (sections 4.2–4.3) (1 pt).
-   The honest estimate is close to 0.5, chance level, give or take about 0.07 for 50 samples (1 pt). Common error: blaming the classifier, or switching to leave-one-out, which keeps the leak.
:::

### Projects {#projects-list}

Every project uses public data, runs on a laptop CPU, and needs only this module and its refreshers; anything that needs a later course is under "Going further". Levels ★/★★/★★★ are those of the exercises, efforts are per student, and all four projects are optional practice.

**Grading grid used by every project of this page** (a project card may replace one row).

| Criterion | Weight |
|---|---|
| Question and success metric stated before the experiments | 10 % |
| Correct use of the course results (cited by number) | 25 % |
| Protocol: leakage-free split, baselines, at least 3 seeds, intervals | 25 % |
| Results and analysis: error analysis, limits, one responsible-AI remark | 20 % |
| Reproducibility: repository, README, pinned environment, one command | 10 % |
| Communication: report (≤ 6 pages solo, ≤ 10 group) or 10-minute oral | 10 % |

Group projects: a contribution statement and an oral with individual questions; the individual grade is the group grade times a factor in [0.8, 1.2].

#### P1 · ★ · solo · Customer segmentation with stable clusters {#proj-1}

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| Goal | Segment the customers of an online retailer from recency, frequency and monetary (RFM) features; for k-means++ and for a Gaussian mixture whose number of components is chosen by BIC, report the cost $W$, the stability (mean adjusted Rand index between 20 seeds and between bootstrap resamples) and the agreement with the baseline of RFM quartile segments. |
| Data | [UCI Online Retail II](https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/502/online+retail+ii) — CC BY 4.0 — 1,067,371 invoice lines of a UK online retailer (2009–2011), 5,942 customers; loading: download the zip from the page, then `pd.concat(pd.read_excel("online_retail_II.xlsx", sheet_name=None).values())` |
| Chapters | [ch. 7](#ch7) (7.1 Lloyd and k-means++, 7.2 EM for Gaussian mixtures, 7.3 PCA for a 2-D view), [ch. 4](#ch4) (4.1 metrics, 4.3 preprocessing inside a pipeline: log-transform, scaling) |
| Deliverables | notebook + 4-page report |
| Effort and compute | ≈ 10 h per student · laptop CPU, longest run ≤ 5 min |
| Objectives served | O6 (e-commerce: segmentation), O7 (an industrial analysis pipeline) |
| Specific criterion | Stability protocol — seeds, bootstrap of customers, sensitivity to the number of clusters — replaces the "Protocol" row (25 %), since clustering has no test labels |
| Responsible AI | Customer IDs are pseudonymous: publish segment profiles only in aggregate and never try to re-identify a customer. |
| Going further | Segment on 2009–2010 and measure how the customers of 2010–2011 move between segments. |

#### P2 · ★★ · solo · Credit default, calibrated and audited {#proj-2}

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| Goal | Predict default on the next payment; for logistic regression (baseline) and gradient boosting, report PR-AUC, Brier score and a reliability diagram before and after Platt and isotonic calibration, and the FPR and FNR per sex and per age band with 95% intervals. |
| Data | [UCI Default of Credit Card Clients](https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/350/default+of+credit+card+clients) — CC BY 4.0 — 30,000 clients of a Taiwanese bank (2005), 23 features, 22% defaults; loading: `from ucimlrepo import fetch_ucirepo; d = fetch_ucirepo(id=350)` |
| Chapters | [ch. 3.1](#ch3) (logistic regression), [ch. 4](#ch4) (4.1 metrics, 4.3 leakage, 4.4 imbalance, 4.5 calibration, [4.8](#fairness) fairness and per-slice intervals), [ch. 6.3](#ch6) (boosting) |
| Deliverables | notebook + 4-page report |
| Effort and compute | ≈ 18 h per student · laptop CPU, longest run ≤ 10 min |
| Objectives served | O6 (finance: credit risk), O8 (calibration and a fairness audit) |
| Specific criterion | Calibration measured on a held-out fold before and after each method, with the identity of proposition 4.5 checked per group, replaces the "Results and analysis" row (20 %) |
| Responsible AI | Sex and age are protected attributes; credit scoring is a high-risk use under the EU AI Act. The model is a teaching artefact and must not inform real decisions. |
| Going further | Set the threshold from a cost matrix (a missed default costs five false alarms), then compare one threshold with group-wise thresholds (section 4.8). |

#### P3 · ★★ · solo · Multi-label news tagging: binary relevance versus classifier chains {#proj-3}

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| Goal | On the 20 most frequent topics of RCV1-v2, compare binary relevance (baseline) with ensembles of classifier chains built on logistic regression; report Hamming loss, subset accuracy and micro-F1 with bootstrap intervals, and the gain of the chains on correlated topic pairs. |
| Data | [RCV1-v2](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.datasets.fetch_rcv1.html) (Lewis et al., [JMLR 2004](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/v5/lewis04a.html)) — made available by Reuters for research purposes — 804,414 newswire stories as TF-IDF vectors (47,236 terms, 103 topics); loading: `sklearn.datasets.fetch_rcv1(subset="train")` (23,149 stories; the first call downloads the full set) |
| Chapters | [ch. 3.1](#ch3), [ch. 4](#ch4) (4.1 metrics, 4.2 nested cross-validation), [ch. 9.1](#ch9) (multi-label losses, classifier chains); extends [Ex. 10 and Ex. 13](#ex) from single-label to multi-label text, without redoing them |
| Deliverables | notebook + 4-page report |
| Effort and compute | ≈ 16 h per student · laptop CPU with 16 GB RAM, longest run ≤ 30 min |
| Objectives served | O3 (text classification), O9 (reproducing a research result: Read et al., 2009) |
| Going further | Optimize the chain order; compare with a fine-tuned transformer of [NLP ch. 7](../m1p2-nlp-text-mining/index.html#ch7) (Period 2). |

#### P4 · ★★ · group (3–4) · Molecules with honest splits: the baseline Graph ML must beat {#proj-4}

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| Goal | Predict HIV-replication inhibition from Morgan fingerprints with logistic regression, an RBF-kernel SVM, a random forest and gradient boosting; report ROC-AUC (the OGB metric), PR-AUC and calibration under the random and the official scaffold split, and the drop from one to the other, against the logistic baseline. |
| Data | [ogbg-molhiv](https://ogb.stanford.edu/docs/graphprop/) (OGB, from MoleculeNet) — MIT — 41,127 molecules, about 3.5% active; loading: SMILES, labels and scaffold split from the OGB CSV archive (`csv_mol_download/hiv.zip` on the page), fingerprints with RDKit, `AllChem.GetMorganFingerprintAsBitVect(mol, 2, nBits=2048)` |
| Chapters | [ch. 3](#ch3), [ch. 4](#ch4) (4.2 nested CV, 4.3 leakage — a scaffold is the "same entity" of leak (3), 4.4 imbalance, 4.5 calibration), [ch. 5](#ch5) (kernels), [ch. 6](#ch6) (forests, boosting) |
| Deliverables | repository with one-command run + 8-page report + 10-minute oral with individual questions; each member owns one model family, the protocol is shared |
| Effort and compute | ≈ 18 h per student · laptop CPU; the SVM on a 10,000-molecule subsample or with a Nyström approximation, longest run ≤ 30 min |
| Objectives served | O4 (molecules: the non-graph baseline), O6 (pharma), O7 (team protocol and reproducibility) |
| Going further | A Weisfeiler-Lehman kernel on the molecular graphs, then a GIN in [Graph ML ch. 5](../m1p2-graph-ml/index.html#ch5) (Period 2), on the same scaffold split. |

### End-of-year projects {#projects-capstone}

Every Year-1 integrative project starts from this module: its week-2 milestone is a baseline built with the chapter 4 protocol (leakage-free split, nested cross-validation, at least 3 seeds, intervals), and the subgroup reports of section 4.8 feed each responsible-AI note.

The specific uses are calibration in [Y1-1](../m1-integrative-projects/index.html#y1-1) (drug repurposing); imbalance, calibration and boosting in [Y1-2](../m1-integrative-projects/index.html#y1-2) (illicit transactions); leave-one-event-out validation in [Y1-3](../m1-integrative-projects/index.html#y1-3) (rumours); regression and latent-factor baselines (ch. 2, 7) in [Y1-4](../m1-integrative-projects/index.html#y1-4) (recommendation).

They continue with boosted travel-time models (ch. 4, 6) in [Y1-5](../m1-integrative-projects/index.html#y1-5) (delivery routing); fingerprints and scaffold splits, as in P4, in [Y1-6](../m1-integrative-projects/index.html#y1-6) (molecules); multi-label metrics and calibration (9.1, 4.5) in [Y1-7](../m1-integrative-projects/index.html#y1-7) (chest X-rays); bootstrap intervals in [Y1-8](../m1-integrative-projects/index.html#y1-8) (legal retrieval).

In Year 2, the transverse-project capstones [C2](../m2-projet-transverse/index.html#c2) (calibrated alerts on transaction graphs) and [C6](../m2-projet-transverse/index.html#c6) (tree-ensemble baselines for a force field) reuse the same protocol.

## References {#refs}

### Textbooks

-   T. Hastie, R. Tibshirani, J. Friedman, *The Elements of Statistical Learning*, 2nd ed., Springer, 2009 — [free PDF](https://hastie.su.domains/ElemStatLearn/): the reference textbook of the course.
-   G. James, D. Witten, T. Hastie, R. Tibshirani, *An Introduction to Statistical Learning*, 2nd ed., Springer, 2021 — the applied (Python) version of the same foundation.
-   C. Bishop, *Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning*, Springer, 2006 — for the generative viewpoint (EM, kernels) taken up again in Deep Learning.
-   S. Shalev-Shwartz, S. Ben-David, *Understanding Machine Learning*, Cambridge, 2014 — ch. 6 (VC dimension and Sauer's lemma), ch. 26 (Rademacher complexity), ch. 13 (margin bounds, SVM).
-   K. Murphy, *Probabilistic Machine Learning: An Introduction*, MIT Press, 2022 — a modern panorama, free online.
-   S. Boucheron, G. Lugosi, P. Massart, *Concentration Inequalities: A Nonasymptotic Theory of Independence*, Oxford University Press, 2013 — ch. 1-2: Markov, Hoeffding, Chernoff, and beyond (chapter 0).
-   G. Garrigos, R. M. Gower, *Handbook of Convergence Theorems for (Stochastic) Gradient Methods*, [arXiv:2301.11235](https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.11235), 2023 — rates of gradient descent and SGD (section 0.2).
-   [scikit-learn User Guide](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/user_guide.html) — the labs follow its conventions (pipelines, calibration, imblearn for imbalance).
-   S. Boyd, L. Vandenberghe, *Convex Optimization*, Cambridge University Press, 2004 — [free PDF](https://web.stanford.edu/~boyd/cvxbook/): Lagrangian duality, Slater's condition and the KKT conditions (section 0.3).

Friedman, *Greedy Function Approximation: A Gradient Boosting Machine*, Annals of Statistics 29(5), 2001 — [Project Euclid](https://projecteuclid.org/journals/annals-of-statistics/volume-29/issue-5/Greedy-function-approximation-A-gradient-boosting-machine/10.1214/aos/1013203451.short): boosting as functional gradient descent (chapter 6).
